meta.title: Scarlet Thread timeline
notes: Years are whole numbers. A year before Christ (BC) is negative and a year AD is positive, so 1446 BC is -1446.
date.display is the wording the reader sees. Every early date carries c. for about. Write ranges with the word to, never with a dash.
date.start is null only for an entry Scripture does not date. Those are drawn in a box marked as not dated. Nothing from Genesis 1 to 11 carries a year.
certainty is one of firm, approximate, disputed, traditional, undated.
Where scholars differ, the entry keeps the primary date and lists the other view under alternatives. An alternative with a start year is also drawn on the timeline as a dashed marker.
The early date of the Exodus (c. 1446 BC, from 1 Kings 6:1) is primary. The late date (c. 1260s BC) is always shown beside it.
nodes lists the map stops an entry belongs to. books limits an entry to one map. An entry with no books key shows on every map.
Sources are named at the level of the work. Do not add a page number, a date, or an event that has not been checked.
books uses the map keys advent, deuteronomy, isaiah_book, and revelation. The Isaiah key is isaiah_book because the Advent map already has a stop with the id isaiah.

certainty.firm: Well attested. Some books differ by a year.
certainty.approximate: An approximate date. The c. stands for about.
certainty.disputed: Scholars differ. The other view is given with it.
certainty.traditional: A tradition, not a certain record.
certainty.undated: Scripture gives no date, so this timeline gives none.

events.label: The first gospel promise
events.note: God speaks this promise in the garden, at the very start of the Bible's story. Scripture gives no dates for Genesis 1 to 11, and Christians who trust the Bible count those years differently. This timeline leaves them undated.
events.source: Genesis 3:15

events.label: Abraham
events.note: God promises that all the nations will be blessed in Abraham's offspring. These years come from adding the ages in Genesis and counting back from the early date of the Exodus. They are approximate.

alternatives.note: Many scholars place Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob later, somewhere in these centuries.

events.source: Genesis 21:5; Genesis 22:18; Genesis 25:7; Genesis 25:26; Genesis 47:9; Exodus 12:40; 1 Kings 6:1

events.label: Jacob blesses Judah
events.note: Near his death in Egypt, Jacob says the scepter will not depart from Judah. The year is counted back from the early date of the Exodus, using the 430 years of Exodus 12:40 and Jacob's 17 years in Egypt. It is approximate.

alternatives.display: Later, by one to two centuries
alternatives.note: The year is later if the Exodus is dated late, or if the 430 years are counted from Abraham, as some read Galatians 3:17.

events.source: Genesis 47:28; Genesis 49:8-12; Exodus 12:40

events.label: The Exodus from Egypt
events.note: God brings Israel out of slavery in Egypt. 1 Kings 6:1 says Solomon began the temple in the 480th year after the Exodus, and Solomon's fourth year was c. 966 BC. That gives c. 1446 BC. This is called the early date, and this map follows it.

alternatives.label: The Exodus (late date view)
alternatives.note: Many scholars prefer a late date in the 1200s BC, in the reign of Ramesses II. They point to the store city named Raamses in Exodus 1:11 and to their reading of the archaeology. Christians who trust the Bible hold both views.

events.source: Exodus 12:40-41; 1 Kings 6:1; Judges 11:26

events.label: The law given at Mount Sinai
events.note: In the third month after leaving Egypt, Israel camps at Mount Sinai, which Deuteronomy calls Horeb. There God speaks the Ten Commandments. Moses repeats them in Deuteronomy 5.

alternatives.note: This is the year on the late date of the Exodus.

events.source: Exodus 19:1; Exodus 20:1-17; Deuteronomy 5:2-22

events.label: Forty years in the wilderness
events.note: Israel lives in the wilderness for forty years between Egypt and the promised land. Moses says God was humbling and testing them, and feeding them with manna.

alternatives.note: These are the years on the late date of the Exodus.

events.source: Numbers 14:33-34; Deuteronomy 8:2-5

events.label: Moses preaches Deuteronomy
events.note: In the fortieth year after the Exodus, in the eleventh month, Moses preaches to Israel on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan River. The book of Deuteronomy is that preaching.

alternatives.label: Deuteronomy (late date view)
alternatives.note: This is forty years after the late date of the Exodus.

events.source: Deuteronomy 1:1-5

events.label: The death of Moses
events.note: Moses sees the promised land from Mount Nebo and dies there, in the land of Moab. Joshua leads Israel across the Jordan soon after.

alternatives.note: This is the year on the late date of the Exodus.

events.source: Deuteronomy 34:1-8

events.label: God's covenant with David
events.note: David reigns forty years. During that reign God promises him a house and a throne that will last forever. The exact year of the promise is not given, so the whole reign is shown.
events.source: 2 Samuel 5:4-5; 2 Samuel 7:12-16. The reign is counted back from the division of the kingdom, c. 930 BC, as dated in Edwin R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings.

events.label: Solomon begins the temple
events.note: Solomon begins to build the temple in the fourth year of his reign. 1 Kings 6:1 counts this as the 480th year after the Exodus, which is where the early date of the Exodus comes from.
events.source: 1 Kings 6:1. Solomon's years follow Edwin R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings.

events.label: Isaiah the prophet
events.note: Isaiah is called in the year King Uzziah dies, c. 740 BC, and prophesies through the reign of Hezekiah, who dies c. 686 BC. The promise of a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11) comes from these years. Its exact year is not known.
events.source: Isaiah 1:1; Isaiah 6:1; Isaiah 11:1-10. The kings' years follow Edwin R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings.

events.label: The Immanuel sign
events.note: The kings of Syria and Israel attack Judah. Isaiah gives King Ahaz a sign: a virgin will bear a son and call his name Immanuel.
events.source: Isaiah 7:1-17; 2 Kings 16:5-9

events.label: Unto us a child is born
events.note: Isaiah speaks this promise in the years when Assyria overruns Galilee, the land of Zebulun and Naphtali. The exact year is not given.
events.source: Isaiah 9:1-7; 2 Kings 15:29

events.label: Micah names Bethlehem
events.note: Micah prophesies in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, at the same time as Isaiah. He says a ruler for Israel will come from Bethlehem. The exact year of this saying is not given.
events.source: Micah 1:1; Micah 5:2

events.label: Gabriel's announcement to Mary
events.note: In Nazareth the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear the Son of God. Luke does not give the year. It comes shortly before the birth of Jesus.

events.label: The birth of Jesus
events.note: Jesus is born in Bethlehem while Herod the Great is king, and Herod dies in 4 BC. So the birth is usually placed c. 6 to 4 BC. Our calendar counts from a birth year worked out about five hundred years later by a monk named Dionysius Exiguus, and his count was a few years off.

alternatives.note: A few scholars date Herod's death to 1 BC, which would allow a birth c. 3 to 2 BC.

events.source: Matthew 2:1; Luke 2:1-7; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 17

events.label: The magi seek the king
events.note: Wise men from the east come to Jerusalem and then to Bethlehem while Herod is still alive. Matthew 2:16 suggests this may be some time after the birth, up to two years.
events.source: Matthew 2:1-16

events.label: Jesus is tested in the wilderness
events.note: After his baptism Jesus fasts forty days in the wilderness and answers the devil three times from Deuteronomy. Luke dates the preaching of John the Baptist to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, c. AD 28 or 29, or a little earlier if the years are counted from when Tiberius began to share the rule.
events.source: Luke 3:1-2; Luke 3:21-23; Matthew 4:1-11

events.label: The public ministry of Jesus
events.note: Jesus preaches, heals, and teaches. In these years he says, "I am the bread of life." The ministry begins c. AD 27 to 29 and ends at the cross, c. AD 30 or 33.
events.source: Luke 3:1-2; Luke 3:23; John 6:35

events.label: The cross and the resurrection
events.note: Jesus is crucified under Pontius Pilate at Passover and rises on the third day. In the days just before, he teaches in the temple and names the great commandment. Pilate governed c. AD 26 to 36. Within those years, AD 30 and AD 33 are the two dates most often defended, and scholars are divided between them. The bar covers both years. It does not mean the events lasted three years.

alternatives.note: Both dates are held by scholars who trust the Gospels. This map does not choose between them.

events.source: Matthew 22:34-40; Matthew 27:1 to 28:10; Luke 23:1 to 24:12; John 19:1 to 20:18; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4

events.label: Peter preaches in the temple
events.note: Soon after Pentecost, Peter tells the crowd at Solomon's Portico that Jesus is the prophet Moses promised. Stephen repeats the same promise in Acts 7:37. The year follows the date of the cross, so it is AD 30 or AD 33.

alternatives.note: The year depends on the date of the cross. This map does not choose between them.

events.source: Acts 3:11-26; Acts 7:37

events.label: Paul writes Galatians
events.note: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.

alternatives.display: c. AD 48 to 49, or c. AD 53 to 55
alternatives.note: Some date the letter early, before the Jerusalem council of Acts 15. Others date it several years later. The bar covers both views.

events.source: Galatians 1:1-2; Galatians 3:10-14; Acts 13:1 to 15:35

events.label: Paul writes Romans
events.note: Paul writes to the church in Rome near the end of his third missionary journey, probably from Corinth, just before he carries a gift to Jerusalem.
events.source: Romans 15:25-26; Romans 16:1; Acts 20:2-3

events.label: Third Dynasty of Ur
events.note: A Sumerian kingdom ruled from the city of Ur in Mesopotamia, in what is now southern Iraq. Genesis names Ur of the Chaldeans as Abraham's first home. The dates follow the commonly used middle chronology. Other systems move them by several decades.
events.source: Marc Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East; Genesis 11:31

events.label: Egypt's Middle Kingdom
events.note: A long, settled age in Egypt, centuries after the great pyramids were built. On the early dates, Joseph and then Jacob come to Egypt in this period.
events.source: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt

events.label: Hammurabi of Babylon
events.note: King of Babylon, known for his collection of laws carved on stone. The dates follow the commonly used middle chronology. Other systems move them several decades earlier or later.
events.source: Marc Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East; the stele of Hammurabi, Louvre Museum

events.label: Hyksos kings in Egypt
events.note: Rulers from western Asia hold the north of Egypt until the Egyptians drive them out.
events.source: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt

events.label: The Hittite kingdom
events.note: A great power ruled from Hattusa, in what is now central Turkey. For a time it rivaled Egypt.
events.source: Trevor Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites

events.label: Egypt's New Kingdom
events.note: Egypt's age of empire, with pharaohs such as Thutmose III, Amenhotep II, and Ramesses II. The Exodus falls in this period on either date. The Bible does not name the pharaoh.
events.source: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt

events.label: Pharaoh Thutmose III
events.note: One of Egypt's strongest pharaohs. On the early date of the Exodus, he or his son Amenhotep II (c. 1427 to 1400 BC) is often suggested as the pharaoh of Moses' day. The Bible does not name him, so this is a suggestion and not a fact.
events.source: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt

events.label: Pharaoh Ramesses II
events.note: Egypt's great builder. On the late date of the Exodus he is usually taken to be the pharaoh. The Bible does not name him, so this is a suggestion and not a fact.
events.source: Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt

events.label: The Merneptah Stele
events.note: A victory stone of Pharaoh Merneptah, the son of Ramesses II. It holds the earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible, as a people already living in Canaan.
events.source: The Merneptah Stele, Egyptian Museum, Cairo; Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt

events.label: The Assyrian Empire
events.note: The great power of Isaiah's day. Its heartland, with cities such as Nineveh, lies in what is now northern Iraq.
events.source: Amélie Kuhrt, The Ancient Near East, c. 3000 to 330 BC

events.label: Rome founded (by tradition)
events.note: This is the year the Romans themselves gave for the founding of their city. It is a tradition and not a record.
events.source: The reckoning of the Roman scholar Varro; The Oxford Classical Dictionary

events.label: Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria
events.note: He conquers Syria and much of northern Israel, including Galilee. King Ahaz of Judah sends to him for help.
events.source: 2 Kings 15:29; 2 Kings 16:7-9; Amélie Kuhrt, The Ancient Near East, c. 3000 to 330 BC

events.label: The fall of Samaria
events.note: Assyria takes Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, and carries its people into exile. Some books give 721 BC.
events.source: 2 Kings 17:5-6; 2 Kings 18:9-12; Edwin R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings

events.label: Sennacherib invades Judah
events.note: The king of Assyria takes the towns of Judah and threatens Jerusalem in the reign of Hezekiah. The Lord delivers the city. Sennacherib's own record of the campaign survives.
events.source: 2 Kings 18:13 to 19:37; Isaiah 36:1 to 37:38; the Taylor Prism, British Museum

events.label: The Babylonian Empire
events.note: Babylon rises as Assyria falls. Its greatest king, Nebuchadnezzar II, reigns 605 to 562 BC. The ruins of Babylon are in Iraq, south of Baghdad.
events.source: Amélie Kuhrt, The Ancient Near East, c. 3000 to 330 BC; the Babylonian Chronicles, British Museum

events.label: The fall of Nineveh
events.note: The Babylonians and the Medes destroy Nineveh, the Assyrian capital. The prophet Nahum had announced its fall.
events.source: Nahum 3:1-7; the Babylonian Chronicles, British Museum

events.label: The fall of Jerusalem
events.note: Nebuchadnezzar destroys Jerusalem and Solomon's temple and carries Judah into exile in Babylon.

alternatives.note: Scholars differ by one year, because of how the years of the kings are counted. Both 587 and 586 BC are widely used.

events.source: 2 Kings 25:1-21; Jeremiah 52:12-30; Edwin R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings

events.label: The Persian Empire
events.note: The empire of Cyrus and his heirs, the setting of Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther. Persia is modern Iran.
events.source: Amélie Kuhrt, The Ancient Near East, c. 3000 to 330 BC

events.label: Cyrus takes Babylon
events.note: Cyrus the Great of Persia conquers Babylon. In his first year over Babylon he lets the exiles of Judah go home to rebuild the temple.
events.source: Ezra 1:1-4; Isaiah 44:28 to 45:1; the Nabonidus Chronicle and the Cyrus Cylinder, British Museum

events.label: Alexander the Great
events.note: The king of Macedon conquers the Persian Empire and takes the land of Judea in 332 BC. Greek becomes the common language of the region. The New Testament was later written in it.
events.source: Arrian, The Anabasis of Alexander; The Oxford Classical Dictionary

events.label: Greek kingdoms rule Judea
events.note: After Alexander dies his generals divide his empire. The Ptolemies of Egypt hold Judea from c. 301 BC. The Seleucids of Syria take it c. 200 BC.
events.source: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 12; The Oxford Classical Dictionary

events.label: The Maccabees
events.note: The Seleucid king Antiochus IV outlaws Jewish worship and defiles the temple. Judas Maccabeus and his family lead a revolt, and the temple is rededicated in 164 BC. John 10:22 mentions the feast that remembers it. The family, called the Hasmoneans, leads Judea until Rome arrives. The books of Maccabees are useful history. They are not part of Scripture.
events.source: 1 Maccabees 1:1 to 4:61; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 12 to 13

events.label: Rome takes Jerusalem
events.note: The Roman general Pompey captures Jerusalem. From this point Judea is under the power of Rome.
events.source: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 14

events.label: Herod the Great
events.note: Rome names Herod king of Judea in 40 BC, and he takes Jerusalem in 37 BC. He rebuilds the temple on a grand scale. He is the King Herod of Matthew 2.

alternatives.note: Most scholars date Herod's death to 4 BC. A few argue for 1 BC.

events.source: Matthew 2:1-19; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 14 to 17

events.label: Caesar Augustus
events.note: The first Roman emperor. Luke 2:1 names him as the ruler whose decree brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem.
events.source: Luke 2:1; Suetonius, The Life of Augustus; The Oxford Classical Dictionary

events.label: The census of Quirinius
events.note: Luke 2:2 links the registration at the birth of Jesus with Quirinius, governor of Syria. Outside the Bible, the census of Quirinius that we know of took place in AD 6, about ten years after Herod died. How the two fit together is debated.

alternatives.display: An earlier registration, c. 6 to 4 BC
alternatives.note: Some suggest an earlier registration that no other record preserves. Others translate Luke 2:2 as the registration before Quirinius was governor. This map notes the question and does not settle it.

events.source: Luke 2:1-2; Acts 5:37; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18

events.label: Emperor Tiberius
events.note: The emperor during the ministry of John the Baptist and of Jesus. Luke 3:1 dates John's preaching by his reign.
events.source: Luke 3:1; Tacitus, Annals 1 to 6

events.label: Pontius Pilate governs Judea
events.note: The Roman governor who sentenced Jesus to the cross. The Roman historian Tacitus mentions it, and a stone found at Caesarea in 1961 carries Pilate's name.
events.source: Luke 3:1; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18; Tacitus, Annals 15.44; the Pilate Stone, Israel Museum

events.label: Emperor Nero
events.note: The emperor when Paul wrote Romans. Early Christian writers say that Peter and Paul were put to death in Rome under him.
events.source: Tacitus, Annals 13 to 16; Eusebius, Church History 2.25

events.label: Rome destroys the temple
events.note: After a Jewish revolt that began in AD 66, the Roman general Titus takes Jerusalem and burns the temple. Jesus had said that not one stone would be left on another.
events.source: Josephus, The Jewish War 5 to 6; Matthew 24:1-2

events.label: King Uzziah dies
events.note: Uzziah, also called Azariah, had reigned over Judah for fifty-two years. In the year he died, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting on a throne and was sent to preach. Some books give 739 BC.
events.source: Isaiah 6:1; 2 Kings 15:1-7; 2 Chronicles 26:1-23. The year follows Edwin R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings.

events.label: Hezekiah and Sennacherib
events.note: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib of Assyria takes the fortified towns of Judah and threatens Jerusalem. Hezekiah prays, Isaiah brings God's answer, and the LORD delivers the city. The world history track shows the same year from the Assyrian side.
events.source: Isaiah 36:1 to 37:38; 2 Kings 18:13 to 19:37; the Taylor Prism, British Museum

events.label: Isaiah 40 to 66
events.note: These chapters speak comfort to exiles in Babylon and name Cyrus, about 150 years ahead of his time. On the view this map follows, Isaiah the son of Amoz wrote them during his own ministry, and many who hold this view place them late in his life. The exact years are not known, so the whole ministry is shown.

alternatives.label: Isaiah 40 to 66 (later date view)
alternatives.note: Many modern scholars hold that chapters 40 to 55 were written by an unnamed prophet among the exiles shortly before Cyrus took Babylon, and chapters 56 to 66 later still. The New Testament quotes both halves of the book as Isaiah's. John 12:38-41 quotes Isaiah 53 and Isaiah 6 together and names Isaiah for both.

events.source: Isaiah 1:1; Isaiah 40:1-2; Isaiah 44:28; John 12:38-41

events.label: Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD
events.note: Ezekiel dates this vision to the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin, who was taken to Babylon in 597 BC. Ezekiel was among the exiles by the Chebar canal in Babylonia, in what is now Iraq.
events.source: Ezekiel 1:1-3; 2 Kings 24:10-16; the Babylonian Chronicles, British Museum

events.label: Ezekiel's vision of the temple river
events.note: Ezekiel dates his vision of a new temple to the twenty-fifth year of the exile, the fourteenth year after Jerusalem fell. The river that flows from the temple is part of that vision.
events.source: Ezekiel 40:1; Ezekiel 47:1-12

events.label: Daniel's vision of the four beasts
events.note: Daniel dates this dream to the first year of Belshazzar, who ruled in Babylon for his father, King Nabonidus. That year is usually placed c. 553 BC, and some place it a few years later. This map follows the book's own dating.

alternatives.label: Daniel (late date view)
alternatives.note: Many modern scholars hold that the book of Daniel reached its present form in the time of the Maccabees, four centuries after the events it tells.

events.source: Daniel 7:1; the Nabonidus Chronicle, British Museum

events.label: Zechariah's night visions
events.note: Zechariah dates his visions to the eleventh month of the second year of Darius, king of Persia, which falls early in 519 BC. The exiles had come home and were rebuilding the temple. It was finished about four years later.
events.source: Zechariah 1:7; Zechariah 4:1-14; Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:15

events.label: Jesus begins to preach in Galilee
events.note: After John the Baptist is arrested, Jesus makes his home in Capernaum and preaches through Galilee. In the synagogue at Nazareth he reads from Isaiah 61. Luke dates the preaching of John the Baptist to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, c. AD 28 or 29, or a little earlier if the years are counted from when Tiberius began to share the rule.
events.source: Matthew 4:12-17; Luke 3:1-2; Luke 4:14-21

events.label: Philip and the Ethiopian official
events.note: Acts gives no year. The meeting comes after the death of Stephen and before the conversion of Saul, within a few years of the cross, which is dated AD 30 or AD 33. The bar covers the range usually given.

events.label: Peter writes his first letter
events.note: Peter writes to Christians scattered across what is now Turkey. He sends greetings from Babylon, which most readers take as a name for Rome. The letter is usually placed shortly before his death under Nero. Scholars who doubt that Peter wrote it date it later.
events.source: 1 Peter 1:1; 1 Peter 5:12-13; Eusebius, Church History 2.25

events.label: John writes Revelation on Patmos
events.note: John sees these visions on the island of Patmos and sends them to seven churches in the province of Asia. Irenaeus, writing c. AD 180, says the vision was seen toward the end of the reign of Domitian, who died in AD 96. Most scholars follow him, and so does this map. The date marks when John saw the visions. It does not mark when the things he saw take place.

alternatives.label: Revelation (early date view)
alternatives.note: A minority of scholars date the book before the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, in or just after the reign of Nero. They point to the measuring of the temple in Revelation 11:1-2 and to the words about what must soon take place. Christians who trust the Bible hold both views.

events.source: Revelation 1:1-3; Revelation 1:9-11; Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3; Eusebius, Church History 3.18

events.label: Emperor Domitian
events.note: The Roman emperor at the time most scholars place the writing of Revelation. Early Christian writers remember him as a persecutor of the church. Historians today differ on how wide that persecution was.
events.source: Suetonius, The Life of Domitian; Eusebius, Church History 3.17 to 3.20; The Oxford Classical Dictionary

places.label: Ur
places.note: Abraham's first home. It is usually identified with the ruins at Tell el-Muqayyar, near Nasiriyah in southern Iraq. A few scholars look for Abraham's Ur farther north, nearer Haran.
places.source: Genesis 11:28-31; the excavations of Leonard Woolley at Ur, 1922 to 1934

places.label: Canaan
places.modern: Israel, the West Bank, and Gaza
places.note: The land God promised to Abraham. It is roughly modern Israel, the West Bank, and Gaza, and it reaches north into Lebanon.

places.label: Mount Sinai (Horeb)
places.note: A long Christian tradition identifies it with Jebel Musa in the south of the Sinai Peninsula, where Saint Catherine's Monastery stands. The Bible does not fix the spot, and other sites have been proposed.
places.source: Exodus 19:1-2; Deuteronomy 5:2; The Oxford Bible Atlas

places.label: The plains of Moab
places.modern: Jordan, east of the Jordan River
places.note: Where Moses preached Deuteronomy. The plains lie in modern Jordan, across the river from Jericho, just north of the Dead Sea.

places.label: Mount Nebo
places.note: Where Moses saw the land and died. It is traditionally identified with a ridge near Madaba in Jordan that looks across the Jordan valley toward Jericho.

places.label: Bethlehem
places.modern: The West Bank, just south of Jerusalem
places.note: The town of David and the birthplace of Jesus. It is still a living town with the same name, a few miles south of Jerusalem.

places.label: Nazareth
places.note: The town in Galilee where Gabriel came to Mary and where Jesus grew up. It is a city in northern Israel today.

places.label: Jerusalem
places.note: David's capital and the city of the temple. It stands on the same hills today.

places.label: Assyria and Nineveh
places.note: The Assyrian heartland lay along the Tigris River. The ruins of Nineveh are across the river from the modern city of Mosul.
places.source: 2 Kings 19:36; Amélie Kuhrt, The Ancient Near East, c. 3000 to 330 BC

places.label: Babylon
places.note: The city of Nebuchadnezzar and the place of Judah's exile. Its ruins are near the modern city of Hillah in Iraq.
places.source: 2 Kings 25:8-11; Amélie Kuhrt, The Ancient Near East, c. 3000 to 330 BC

places.label: Persia
places.note: The homeland of Cyrus. The country was known as Persia in the West until the twentieth century and is now called Iran.
places.source: Ezra 1:1; Amélie Kuhrt, The Ancient Near East, c. 3000 to 330 BC

places.label: Galatia
places.note: A Roman province in the middle of what is now Turkey. Paul preached in its southern cities, such as Iconium and Lystra.

places.label: Rome
places.note: The capital of the empire, and the home of the church Paul wrote to in Romans. It is the capital of Italy today.

places.label: Galilee
places.note: The hill country and lake shore in the north, once the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali. Capernaum, where Jesus made his home, stood on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. Its ruins can be visited today.

places.label: Patmos
places.modern: Greece, an island in the Aegean Sea
places.note: A small rocky island where John received the visions of Revelation. It belongs to Greece today and lies close to the coast of Turkey, southwest of ancient Ephesus.

places.label: The seven churches of Asia
places.note: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea were cities of the Roman province of Asia. All seven sites are in western Turkey. Smyrna is the modern city of Izmir, Pergamum is Bergama, Thyatira is Akhisar, and Philadelphia is Alaşehir. Ephesus, Sardis, and Laodicea are ruins, near Selçuk, Sart, and Denizli.
places.source: Revelation 1:11; Revelation 2:1 to 3:22; The Oxford Bible Atlas
